why.correct: The celiac ganglion is the highest of the three collateral ganglia in front of the vertebral column. It receives the greater splanchnic nerve and supplies the stomach, liver, pancreas and spleen.
options: Correct. This is the celiac ganglion, the collateral ganglion that the greater splanchnic nerve runs to.
The superior cervical ganglion is the top ganglion of the sympathetic chain, in the neck beside the vertebral column. It supplies the head, not the stomach.
The inferior mesenteric ganglion is the lowest collateral ganglion, fed by lumbar fibers. It supplies the end of the colon, the rectum, the bladder and the genitals.
The superior mesenteric ganglion sits below the celiac ganglion and receives the lesser splanchnic nerve. It supplies most of the intestines.

why.correct: The white ramus communicans carries myelinated preganglionic fibers from the spinal nerve into the sympathetic chain. The myelin makes it look white. White rami exist only at T1–L2.
options: The gray ramus carries unmyelinated postganglionic fibers the other way, from the chain back into the spinal nerve. The pinned branch carries the fiber into the chain.
Correct. This is the white ramus, the route by which the preganglionic fiber enters the chain.
A splanchnic nerve leaves the chain toward a collateral ganglion in the abdomen. It does not connect the spinal nerve to the chain.
The ventral ramus is the main branch of the spinal nerve that goes to the front of the trunk and the limbs, not the short link to the chain.

why.correct: White rami communicantes carry myelinated preganglionic fibers from the spinal nerves into the chain ganglia. The myelin makes them look white, and they exist only at T1–L2, where the lateral horn sends sympathetic fibers out.
options: Correct. These are white rami, carrying myelinated preganglionic fibers into the chain.
Dorsal roots carry sensory fibers into the back of the spinal cord. They do not connect to the chain ganglia.
Gray rami carry unmyelinated postganglionic fibers the other way, from the chain back out to every spinal nerve.
Postganglionic fibers leave the chain through gray rami or splanchnic routes. The pinned branches carry fibers into the chain, before the synapse.

why.correct: The ciliary ganglion, behind the eye, is the terminal ganglion for the parasympathetic fibers of the oculomotor nerve. Its short postganglionic fibers narrow the pupil and adjust the lens for near vision.
options: The otic ganglion receives parasympathetic fibers from nerve IX and supplies the largest saliva gland, not the eye.
The superior cervical ganglion is a sympathetic chain ganglion in the neck. Nerve III carries parasympathetic fibers, which never synapse in the chain.
The pterygopalatine ganglion receives fibers from nerve VII and supplies the tear gland and nasal glands.
Correct. This is the ciliary ganglion, the terminal ganglion for nerve III.

why.correct: Sympathetic preganglionic cell bodies sit in the lateral horn of the thoracic and upper lumbar cord, T1–L2. That is why the division is called thoracolumbar.
options: The brainstem and S2–S4 are the parasympathetic (craniosacral) origins.
Correct. The lateral horn of T1–L2 holds every sympathetic preganglionic cell body.
The chain ganglia hold the cell bodies of postganglionic neurons. Preganglionic cell bodies are inside the CNS.
The ventral horn holds somatic motor neurons that supply skeletal muscle, and it runs the whole cord. Sympathetic output starts only at T1–L2.

why.correct: The oculomotor (III), facial (VII), glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) nerves carry the cranial parasympathetic outflow. The rest of the parasympathetic outflow leaves from S2–S4.
options: Correct. Remember them as 3, 7, 9 and 10.
The trigeminal nerve (V) is sensory to the face and motor to the chewing muscles. It carries no parasympathetic preganglionic fibers of its own.
Nerves IV and VI are purely somatic motor nerves to eye muscles. Of the eye-movement nerves, only nerve III carries parasympathetic fibers.
Nerves I, II and VIII are sensory nerves for smell, vision, and hearing and balance. They carry no motor output at all.

why.correct: The preganglionic axon leaves the lateral horn by the ventral root, turns into the chain through a white ramus (often climbing a few levels), and synapses in a chain ganglion. The unmyelinated postganglionic axon rejoins a spinal nerve through a gray ramus and rides that nerve to the skin.

Fibers to the adrenal medulla are preganglionic all the way: they pass through both the chain and the celiac ganglion without synapsing. Chromaffin cells take the place of postganglionic neurons, but they release their product into the blood, so it acts as a hormone.

The parasympathetic division is craniosacral, uses terminal or intramural ganglia in or beside its targets, so its preganglionic fibers are long and postganglionic fibers short, and about three quarters of its fibers travel in the vagus nerve. It has no chain and no gray rami.
options: Correct. Nerves III, VII, IX and X, plus S2–S4.
Correct. These are the terminal and intramural ganglia.
Gray rami carry sympathetic postganglionic fibers. Parasympathetic fibers do not reach the skin.
Correct. The ganglion sits at the target, so the first neuron covers almost the whole distance.
Branching through the chain is the sympathetic pattern. Parasympathetic preganglionic neurons contact only a few postganglionic neurons, and there is no parasympathetic chain.
Correct. The vagus carries about three quarters of all parasympathetic preganglionic fibers.

why.correct: Gray rami carry unmyelinated sympathetic postganglionic fibers from the chain back into spinal nerves. Their preganglionic neurons sit in the upper thoracic cord; the fibers climbed the chain to a cervical ganglion before synapsing.
options: Preganglionic fibers enter the chain through white rami, and there are no white rami at C6 because no sympathetic fibers leave the cord there.
The parasympathetic division does not supply the limbs and has no fibers in the gray rami.
Somatic motor fibers leave in the ventral root and stay in the spinal nerve. They do not pass through the rami communicantes.
Correct. A gray ramus at any level carries postganglionic sympathetic fibers back into the spinal nerve.

why.correct: The sympathetic supply to the whole head leaves the cord at T1–T2 and climbs the chain to the superior cervical ganglion. A tumor at the lung apex can compress the chain there. The eye muscle that widens the pupil, a small smooth muscle in the eyelid and the facial sweat glands all lose their sympathetic input, so the pupil is small, the lid droops and the skin stays dry.
options: Oculomotor damage would remove the parasympathetic fibers that narrow the pupil, so the pupil would be large, not small. It would also paralyze several eye movements.
Correct. Losing sympathetic input to the head produces a small pupil, a slightly drooping lid and loss of facial sweating on that side.
The vagus nerve supplies the organs of the chest and abdomen. It does not supply the pupil, the eyelid or the sweat glands of the face.
The facial nerve's parasympathetic fibers go to the tear and saliva glands, and its motor fibers to the muscles of facial expression. Facial sweat glands get only sympathetic fibers.

why.correct: Fibers bound for the abdominal organs pass through the chain without synapsing. They synapse in a collateral ganglion, here the celiac ganglion, after traveling in a splanchnic nerve.
options: This step is right. T7 lies within the T1–L2 outflow and feeds the greater splanchnic nerve.
This step is right. Every preganglionic fiber enters the chain through a white ramus.
This is the error. Splanchnic fibers pass through the chain ganglia without synapsing.
This step is right. The greater splanchnic nerve (about T5–T9) runs to the celiac ganglion.
This step is right. The synapse happens in the celiac ganglion, and the postganglionic fiber runs to the stomach.

why.correct: Preganglionic fibers synapse directly on chromaffin cells in the adrenal medulla, which release epinephrine and some norepinephrine into the blood.
options: Correct. Chromaffin cells stand in for postganglionic neurons.
Fibers to the adrenal medulla pass through the celiac ganglion without synapsing. If they synapsed there, the second neuron would release its transmitter onto an organ, not into the blood.
Gray rami carry postganglionic fibers back to spinal nerves, toward the skin and limbs. They are not on the route to the adrenal gland.
The outer layer of the adrenal gland is controlled by hormones, not by sympathetic fibers. Epinephrine comes from the medulla.

why.correct: A sympathetic preganglionic neuron diverges: it branches up and down the chain and synapses on many postganglionic neurons, often ten or more. The chain links all levels, and the adrenal medulla adds a hormone that reaches every tissue. Parasympathetic preganglionic fibers run to terminal ganglia at single organs and contact only a few postganglionic neurons.
options: Sympathetic postganglionic fibers are unmyelinated. Myelin changes conduction speed, not how many targets a neuron reaches.
The number of neurons alone does not explain the spread. What matters is how widely each preganglionic neuron branches.
Correct. Divergence through the chain spreads one burst across many organs.
Parasympathetic postganglionic fibers are short, because their ganglia sit at the target. That is what keeps their effects local.

why.correct: Skeletal muscle contracts only when a somatic motor neuron excites it, so cutting the nerve paralyzes it. Cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and many glands have their own built-in activity. Autonomic nerves adjust that activity up or down rather than starting it.
options: Correct. The heart beats without nerves; its autonomic supply only changes the rate and strength.
The two neurons are in series, not in parallel. Cutting either one breaks the pathway.
Cut peripheral axons regrow slowly, over weeks to months, and after a transplant the heart stays largely without nerves for a long time.
Cardiac muscle is an autonomic effector. No somatic motor neurons supply it.

why.correct: The vagus nerve leaves the brainstem through the skull and runs to the heart outside the spinal cord, so a cord injury does not touch it. The brain's control of all sympathetic output runs down the cord to the lateral horn at T1–L2, below the cut.
options: The T1–T4 neurons are still alive, but they sit below the cut, so signals from the brain can no longer reach them.
Superior cervical ganglion fibers are sympathetic and start from preganglionic neurons at T1–T2, below the cut. Their control from the brain is lost too.
Correct. The vagus nerve bypasses the spinal cord entirely.
The sacral outflow is below the cut, and it supplies the pelvic organs, not the heart.

why.correct: Vagal preganglionic fibers run all the way to intramural ganglia in the stomach wall, where they synapse on short postganglionic neurons.
options: The celiac ganglion is a sympathetic collateral ganglion. Vagal fibers pass through the nerve network around it without synapsing there.
The chain belongs to the sympathetic division. The parasympathetic division has no chain.
Dorsal root ganglia hold the cell bodies of sensory neurons, not autonomic motor neurons.
Correct. These are intramural ganglia, a type of terminal ganglion.

why.correct: Chromaffin cells develop from the same embryonic tissue as sympathetic postganglionic neurons and are stimulated directly by preganglionic fibers. Having no axons, they release their product into the blood instead of onto a target.
options: Preganglionic neurons are the cells that stimulate chromaffin cells, one step earlier in the pathway.
Correct. They take the place of the second neuron in the sympathetic chain of two.
The adrenal medulla gets no parasympathetic supply, so there is no parasympathetic cell to compare with.
Somatic motor neurons run straight from the CNS to skeletal muscle and are not part of any autonomic pathway.

why.correct: Chromaffin cells release epinephrine into the blood. It keeps circulating and acting for a few minutes after the nerve activity stops, so its effects outlast the burst.
options: Slow conduction delays a signal by a fraction of a second. It cannot make an effect last minutes.
Gray rami do carry fibers to the skin, but that says nothing about how long the effect on the heart lasts.
Correct. The hormone outlasts the nerve signal.
The length of the preganglionic fiber sets where the ganglion is, not how long an effect lasts.

why.correct: The pelvic splanchnic nerves carry the sacral parasympathetic outflow from S2–S4 to the bladder, rectum, last part of the colon and reproductive organs.
options: The stomach gets its parasympathetic supply from the vagus nerve.
The heart gets its parasympathetic supply from the vagus nerve.
The largest saliva gland, in front of the ear, gets its parasympathetic supply from the glossopharyngeal nerve through the otic ganglion.
Correct. The bladder depends on the sacral outflow.

why.correct: Parasympathetic fibers do not travel in the gray rami or spinal nerves, so they never reach the skin or most blood vessels, and they do not supply the adrenal medulla. The heart and the iris get fibers from both divisions.
options: Correct. Sweat glands get sympathetic fibers through the gray rami.
Correct. The arrector pili muscles are supplied only by sympathetic fibers.
Correct. Only sympathetic preganglionic fibers reach the adrenal medulla.
The heart gets sympathetic fibers from the upper thoracic chain and parasympathetic fibers from the vagus.
Correct. Most blood vessels receive only sympathetic fibers.
The iris gets parasympathetic fibers from nerve III, which narrow the pupil, and sympathetic fibers, which widen it.

why.correct: Every preganglionic neuron in both divisions is cholinergic, as is every parasympathetic postganglionic neuron. The one group of cholinergic sympathetic postganglionic neurons supplies the eccrine sweat glands.
options: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons also release acetylcholine, onto nicotinic receptor proteins in the chain and collateral ganglia.
Correct. These are the cholinergic neurons of the ANS.
Most sympathetic postganglionic neurons are adrenergic and release norepinephrine.
Preganglionic neurons to the adrenal medulla are cholinergic, but so are all other preganglionic neurons and all parasympathetic postganglionic neurons.

why.correct: The sympathetic postganglionic neurons to eccrine sweat glands are an exception: they are cholinergic. Their acetylcholine binds muscarinic receptor proteins on the gland cells.
options: Most sympathetic targets do receive norepinephrine, but the eccrine sweat glands are the classic exception.
Circulating epinephrine has only a small effect on eccrine sweating. The nerve supply, using acetylcholine, drives it.
Correct. A sympathetic response carried by acetylcholine on muscarinic receptor proteins.
Nicotinic receptor proteins are in the ganglia and adrenal medulla, not on the sweat gland cells. That is why atropine, a muscarinic blocker, stops sweating.

why.correct: A beta-1 blocker removes the sympathetic push on the heart only. Heart rate and force fall, so blood pressure falls. Targets that respond through alpha or muscarinic receptor proteins, such as the sweat glands and the pupil, are unchanged.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Norepinephrine and epinephrine can no longer bind the beta-1 receptor proteins in the heart's pacemaker tissue, so the cells reach threshold more slowly.

variables.name: Force of each heart contraction
variables.why: Blocked beta-1 receptor proteins on heart muscle cells mean less cyclic AMP and less calcium entry, so each contraction is weaker.

variables.name: Blood pressure
variables.why: A slower, weaker heart pumps less blood into the arteries each minute, so arterial pressure falls.

variables.name: Sweating
variables.why: Eccrine sweat glands respond to acetylcholine on muscarinic receptor proteins, which a beta-1 blocker does not touch.

variables.name: Pupil diameter
variables.why: The pupil is set by alpha-1 receptor proteins on the dilator muscle and muscarinic receptor proteins on the circular muscle, neither of which is blocked.

why.correct: Atropine blocks every muscarinic receptor protein, so it removes all parasympathetic effects and also sympathetic sweating. The heart speeds up, the pupils widen, and the mouth, skin and gut slow down or dry out.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Acetylcholine from the vagus nerve can no longer bind muscarinic receptor proteins on the heart's pacemaker tissue, so its slowing effect is removed and the rate climbs.

variables.name: Pupil diameter
variables.why: The circular iris muscle that narrows the pupil works through muscarinic receptor proteins. With it blocked, the alpha-1 dilator muscle wins and the pupil widens.

variables.name: Volume of saliva
variables.why: Watery saliva is secreted in response to acetylcholine on muscarinic receptor proteins, so the mouth goes dry.

variables.name: Sweating
variables.why: Eccrine sweat glands respond to acetylcholine on muscarinic receptor proteins, even though their nerves are sympathetic, so atropine blocks sweating.

variables.name: Movement of the stomach and intestine wall
variables.why: Parasympathetic acetylcholine speeds gut smooth muscle through muscarinic receptor proteins, so blocking them slows the gut.

why.correct: Albuterol relaxes airway smooth muscle through beta-2 receptor proteins, so the airways widen. The small amount absorbed into the blood causes the typical side effects, shakiness and a faster heart rate. It does not act on the pupil.

variables.name: Tension in the smooth muscle of the small airway walls
variables.why: Albuterol activates beta-2 receptor proteins on the airway smooth muscle, which raises cyclic AMP and makes the muscle relax.

variables.name: Diameter of the small airways
variables.why: As the smooth muscle in their walls relaxes, the airways widen.

variables.name: Hand tremor
variables.why: Some drug is absorbed into the blood and reaches beta-2 receptor proteins on skeletal muscle, which makes the hands shaky.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Absorbed drug acts on beta receptor proteins in the heart, and dilated vessels in muscle lower pressure a little, so the heart rate rises modestly.

variables.name: Pupil diameter
variables.why: The pupil muscles respond through alpha-1 and muscarinic receptor proteins, not beta-2, so the pupil does not change.

why.correct: Acetylcholine builds up at all cholinergic synapses. Atropine blocks only muscarinic receptor proteins, so it reverses the parasympathetic-type effects and the sweating. The twitching and weakness come from acetylcholine acting on nicotinic receptor proteins at the neuromuscular junction, which atropine does not block.
options: Atropine blocks the muscarinic receptor proteins through which acetylcholine slows the heart, so the rate rises.
Saliva secretion is driven by acetylcholine on muscarinic receptor proteins, which atropine blocks.
Airway glands secrete in response to acetylcholine on muscarinic receptor proteins, which atropine blocks. Drying these secretions is the main goal of atropine treatment.
Correct. Skeletal muscle responds through nicotinic receptor proteins, which atropine leaves untouched.

why.correct: Blocking muscarinic receptor proteins removes all parasympathetic effects and also sympathetic sweating. The pupils widen, the heart speeds up, the mouth goes dry, and without sweating the skin becomes hot, dry and flushed.
options: Correct. Eccrine sweat glands need acetylcholine on muscarinic receptor proteins, so sweating stops and heat builds up.
Correct. The circular iris muscle is blocked, so the alpha-1 dilator muscle wins.
Correct. The vagus nerve's slowing effect on the heart is blocked.
Drooling means extra saliva, a muscarinic effect. A muscarinic antagonist does the opposite.
Correct. Watery saliva depends on muscarinic receptor proteins.
Pinpoint pupils come from too much muscarinic activity, as in organophosphate poisoning, the opposite of this child's situation.

why.correct: Propranolol blocks beta-1 and beta-2 receptor proteins. Epinephrine acting on beta-2 receptor proteins keeps airway smooth muscle relaxed; with them blocked, the muscle contracts more easily and her narrow-prone airways close down. A mainly beta-1 blocker such as metoprolol carries less of this risk.
options: Propranolol is an antagonist at beta receptor proteins. It does not activate alpha-1 receptor proteins.
Correct. Losing beta-2 relaxation lets her airway smooth muscle tighten.
Blocking muscarinic receptor proteins would widen the airways, not narrow them.
Slowing the heart at ordinary doses does not flood the lungs. The wheeze points to the airways themselves.

why.correct: Airway smooth muscle relaxes through beta-2 receptor proteins. Norepinephrine binds beta-2 weakly, and few varicosities reach these muscle cells. Epinephrine arriving in the blood binds beta-2 strongly, so the airways widen more.
options: Correct. Beta-2 responses depend mainly on circulating epinephrine.
Epinephrine does not bind muscarinic receptor proteins. It acts on alpha and beta adrenergic receptor proteins.
The adrenal medulla releases epinephrine and some norepinephrine, not acetylcholine.
Alpha-1 receptor proteins make smooth muscle contract, which would narrow airways, not widen them.

why.correct: Alpha-2 receptor proteins on the varicosity form a local negative feedback loop: norepinephrine that binds them lowers cyclic AMP and cuts further release. A drug that activates them mimics a strong feedback signal, so release falls. Clonidine also acts on alpha-2 receptor proteins in the brainstem to cut sympathetic output.
options: Alpha-2 receptor proteins inhibit the varicosity. It is the incoming action potential that opens calcium channels and triggers release.
Many alpha-2 receptor proteins sit on the varicosities themselves, which is how they regulate release.
Correct. Activating alpha-2 receptor proteins turns release down.
Negative feedback turns release down in proportion to the signal. It does not switch release off for good.

why.correct: Most blood vessels, including those of the skin, get no parasympathetic fibers. Stimulating the sympathetic ganglia and the adrenal medulla releases norepinephrine and epinephrine onto their alpha-1 receptor proteins, and nothing pulls the other way.
options: Nicotine stimulates nicotinic receptor proteins in both kinds of ganglia at ordinary doses.
Correct. With no opposing fibers, only the sympathetic effect shows.
Parasympathetic postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine, and they do not supply skin vessels anyway.
Nicotine acts on nicotinic receptor proteins. The alpha-1 activation comes from the norepinephrine and epinephrine that the stimulated neurons and adrenal medulla release.

why.correct: Acetylcholine crosses the ganglionic synapse onto nicotinic receptor proteins. The postganglionic neuron fires, calcium entry at its varicosities releases norepinephrine, and norepinephrine on alpha-1 receptor proteins raises calcium in the smooth muscle, which contracts and narrows the vessel.

Parasympathetic postganglionic neurons are cholinergic: they release acetylcholine, which binds muscarinic receptor proteins. Norepinephrine is the sympathetic transmitter, and it would speed the heart.
options: This step is right. Vagal preganglionic fibers end in terminal ganglia in or on the heart.
This step is right. Ganglionic transmission in both divisions uses nicotinic receptor proteins.
This is the error. The transmitter here is acetylcholine.
This step is right. Muscarinic receptor proteins on the pacemaker tissue open potassium channels.
This step is right. Starting further from threshold, the cells fire later, so the rate falls.

why.correct: Beta-1 receptor proteins couple to a G protein that raises cyclic AMP. The second messenger lets more calcium in through the membrane channels, and more calcium means a stronger contraction.
options: Correct. Cyclic AMP is the beta receptor protein's second messenger.
Opening potassium channels is what muscarinic receptor proteins do on the heart, and it slows the heart rather than strengthening it.
Acetylcholine release belongs to cholinergic neurons, not to a step inside a heart muscle cell.
Hyperpolarization would move the cell away from threshold, the opposite of a sympathetic effect.

why.correct: The radial dilator muscle of the iris carries alpha-1 receptor proteins. An alpha-1 agonist makes it contract and pull the pupil open (mydriasis), which lets the doctor see the retina.
options: The circular muscle responds to acetylcholine on muscarinic receptor proteins. Phenylephrine does not act there.
The dilator muscle carries alpha-1 receptor proteins; that is how sympathetic activity widens the pupil.
An agonist activates the dilator muscle's receptor proteins; it makes the muscle contract, not relax.
Correct. Alpha-1 activation contracts the dilator muscle.

why.correct: Nicotinic receptor proteins are ionotropic: acetylcholine binding opens a channel in the protein itself, sodium enters, and the neuron depolarizes within about a millisecond.
options: G protein–coupled receptors are the metabotropic kind, like muscarinic and adrenergic receptor proteins.
Correct. Binding opens the channel directly.
Voltage-gated channels open in response to a change in membrane potential, not to a transmitter binding.
That enzyme is acetylcholinesterase, which ends the signal. It is not a receptor protein.

why.correct: Blocking all ganglia silences every postganglionic neuron. Most blood vessels are held partly constricted by ongoing sympathetic activity through alpha-1 receptor proteins, and they have no parasympathetic supply. When that sympathetic signal disappears, they dilate and pressure falls, especially on standing.
options: The drug acts on nicotinic receptor proteins in the ganglia, not on muscarinic receptor proteins on the heart.
The ganglionic nicotinic type differs from the muscle type, which is why such drugs leave skeletal muscle working.
The adrenal medulla is stimulated through the same kind of nicotinic receptor protein, so the drug blocks its release instead.
Correct. Removing sympathetic constriction of the vessels is the main effect.

why.correct: Metoprolol acts mainly on beta-1 receptor proteins in the heart, so the beta-2 receptor proteins that keep airway smooth muscle relaxed stay available to epinephrine. Propranolol blocks both.
options: Correct. A mainly beta-1 blocker leaves beta-2 relaxation of the airways largely intact.
Beta-2 activation relaxes airway smooth muscle. Blocking beta-2 lets the muscle tighten, which is the danger.
Propranolol blocks beta-1 and beta-2 receptor proteins, so it acts on the airways too.
Metoprolol is an antagonist, not an agonist. It spares beta-2 rather than activating it.

why.correct: Nicotinic receptor proteins sit wherever a preganglionic neuron or a somatic motor neuron releases acetylcholine: on all postganglionic neurons, on chromaffin cells, and (as a different type) on skeletal muscle.
options: Correct. Every chain and collateral ganglion uses nicotinic transmission.
Correct. Terminal and intramural ganglia use nicotinic transmission too.
Correct. Chromaffin cells are stimulated like postganglionic neurons.
Gut smooth muscle responds to parasympathetic acetylcholine through muscarinic receptor proteins.
Correct. The muscle type of nicotinic receptor protein sits at the end plate.
The vagus slows the heart through muscarinic receptor proteins.

why.correct: Epinephrine binds beta-2 receptor proteins on airway smooth muscle, raising cyclic AMP and relaxing the muscle, so the airways reopen. At the same time, alpha-1 constricts leaky vessels and raises blood pressure, and beta-1 strengthens the heart.
options: Alpha-1 activation constricts blood vessels and helps restore pressure. It does not relax airway smooth muscle.
Correct. Beta-2 relaxes airway smooth muscle.
Beta-1 speeds and strengthens the heart. It does not act on the airways.
Epinephrine does not bind muscarinic receptor proteins, and activating them would narrow the airways.

why.correct: The circular muscle of the iris contracts in response to acetylcholine on muscarinic receptor proteins. Pilocarpine mimics that, so the pupil narrows (miosis). Contraction of the ciliary muscle at the same time helps fluid drain from the eye.
options: The dilator muscle responds through alpha-1 receptor proteins, not muscarinic ones.
A muscarinic agonist makes the circular muscle contract, not relax.
Correct. This is the parasympathetic effect on the pupil.
The ciliary body muscle does respond, but so does the circular muscle of the iris, since both carry muscarinic receptor proteins.

why.correct: On standing, blood pools in the legs. Normally sympathetic norepinephrine on alpha-1 receptor proteins narrows the vessels and holds pressure up. With alpha-1 blocked, the vessels stay wide, pressure to the brain drops, and he feels faint.
options: Prazosin blocks alpha-1 receptor proteins, not beta-1, so his heart can still speed up.
Correct. Alpha-1 constriction is what fails.
Prazosin has no action on muscarinic receptor proteins.
Alpha-1 blockade does not narrow the airways. The problem is in the vessels.

why.correct: The response belongs to the receptor protein, not the transmitter. Skin vessels are dominated by alpha-1 receptor proteins, which raise calcium and contract smooth muscle. Skeletal muscle vessels carry many beta-2 receptor proteins, which raise cyclic AMP and relax it, and epinephrine binds beta-2 far better than norepinephrine does.
options: Both hormones bind the same receptor proteins, alpha and beta. Neither carries an instruction of its own.
Most blood vessels, including those in skeletal muscle, receive no parasympathetic fibers.
Correct. Alpha-1 means contract; beta-2 means relax.
Skin vessels carry plenty of alpha-1 receptor proteins; that is how they constrict.

why.correct: Most blood vessels, including those of the skin, receive only sympathetic fibers. Their diameter is controlled by raising or lowering sympathetic tone.
options: The heart has dual innervation: sympathetic cardiac accelerator nerves and the parasympathetic vagus nerve.
The iris has dual innervation: sympathetic fibers to the dilator muscle and parasympathetic fibers to the circular muscle.
Correct. Skin vessels get sympathetic fibers only.
The stomach wall has dual innervation: vagal fibers speed it, sympathetic fibers slow it.

why.correct: Removing a tone reveals how much it was doing. Blocking the vagus nerve's effect frees the heart from a large brake, so the rate jumps. Blocking beta-1 removes only a small sympathetic push, so the rate falls a little.
options: Correct. Vagal tone dominates the resting heart.
The heart carries beta-1 receptor proteins all the time; exercise and fright act through them. At rest they are simply receiving little norepinephrine.
Atropine blocks muscarinic receptor proteins. It has no action on beta-1 receptor proteins.
The sympathetic division keeps a low resting tone, which is why a beta blocker lowers the rate at all.

why.correct: Immediately, phenylephrine narrows vessels through alpha-1 receptor proteins and blood pressure rises, with no direct effect on the heart. The blood pressure reflex then increases vagal tone and lowers sympathetic tone, so the heart rate falls. Negative feedback corrects only part of the rise, so pressure stays somewhat high while the drug acts.

variables.name: Diameter of skin blood vessels, direct drug effect
variables.why: Phenylephrine activates alpha-1 receptor proteins on vessel smooth muscle, which contracts and narrows the vessels.

variables.name: Blood pressure, direct drug effect
variables.why: Narrower vessels throughout the body raise the pressure the heart must push against, so arterial pressure rises.

variables.name: Heart rate, direct drug effect
variables.why: Phenylephrine does not act on beta-1 receptor proteins, so it does not directly change the heart rate.

variables.name: Vagal output to the heart, a minute later
variables.why: Stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the walls of the large arteries fire more as pressure rises. The medulla oblongata responds by increasing vagal output and reducing sympathetic output.

variables.name: Heart rate, a minute later
variables.why: More vagal tone, acting through muscarinic receptor proteins on the heart, slows the heart below its starting rate.

variables.name: Blood pressure, a minute later
variables.why: The reflex slows the heart and trims sympathetic tone, but the drug is still holding alpha-1 receptor proteins active, so pressure is pulled back only part of the way and stays above its starting value.

why.correct: Fear reaches the hypothalamus from the limbic system and triggers a mass sympathetic discharge with adrenal epinephrine. The nervous system raises heart rate and widens the pupils; the cardiovascular system shifts blood away from the skin and gut; the liver adds glucose to the blood; the airways widen; and gut activity slows.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: The amygdala and hypothalamus drive the brainstem to cut vagal output and raise sympathetic output, and norepinephrine and epinephrine act on beta-1 receptor proteins.

variables.name: Pupil diameter
variables.why: Sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion release norepinephrine onto alpha-1 receptor proteins of the dilator muscle.

variables.name: Blood flow to the skin
variables.why: Vasomotor nerves constrict skin vessels through alpha-1 receptor proteins, so she goes pale.

variables.name: Glucose released into the blood by the liver
variables.why: Epinephrine from the adrenal medulla acts on beta-2 receptor proteins in the liver, which breaks glycogen down to glucose.

variables.name: Movement of the stomach and intestine wall
variables.why: Sympathetic activity slows gut smooth muscle while parasympathetic stimulation of the gut falls.

variables.name: Diameter of the small airways
variables.why: Circulating epinephrine relaxes airway smooth muscle through beta-2 receptor proteins.

why.correct: Vasomotor nerves keep finger skin vessels partly constricted at rest. Firing less lets the smooth muscle relax, and the vessels widen. One division with a resting tone gives two-way control.
options: The vagus nerve does not supply skin vessels, and most blood vessels have no parasympathetic fibers at all.
Correct. Withdrawing sympathetic tone widens the vessels.
Alpha-1 receptor proteins make vessel smooth muscle contract. More sympathetic tone narrows skin vessels.
The hypothalamus widens these vessels through the nervous system, by withdrawing sympathetic tone. Local warmth helps, but it is not the only route.

why.correct: Transplant surgery cuts every autonomic nerve to the heart. Without vagal tone to hold it back, the heart runs at its own built-in rate of about 100 beats a minute. At rest, vagal tone is what normally holds the rate near 60 to 80.
options: A donor heart has a normal set of receptor proteins. The change is explained by the missing nerves.
Cutting the nerves removes sympathetic tone to the heart as well; it cannot raise it.
Correct. The missing vagal brake leaves the heart at its own rate.
Nothing about the transplant makes the adrenal medulla secrete continuously, and he is calm.

why.correct: The afferent limb is the optic nerve; the integration center is in the midbrain, which sends the signal to both sides; the efferent limb is the parasympathetic chain of two neurons in the oculomotor nerve, synapsing in the ciliary ganglion. Acetylcholine on muscarinic receptor proteins contracts the circular muscle.

Her right retina and optic nerve still send the light signal to the midbrain, which drives both Edinger–Westphal nuclei. The left oculomotor nerve is intact, so the left pupil narrows. The right oculomotor nerve cannot carry the parasympathetic output, so the right pupil stays wide.
options: The right pupil needs the right oculomotor nerve to narrow, and that nerve is compressed.
The sensory side works and the midbrain sends the signal to both sides, so the left pupil still responds.
The right pupil's efferent pathway is the damaged one, so the right pupil is the one that fails.
Correct. The input is intact and the midbrain crosses the signal, but only the left efferent pathway works.

why.correct: When pressure falls, the medulla oblongata does the opposite: it reduces vagal output and increases sympathetic output. That is what speeds the heart and constricts the vessels in the last step.
options: This step is right. Gravity pools blood in the leg veins, so less returns to the heart and arterial pressure dips.
This step is right. Lower pressure stretches the artery walls less, so their sensory receptors fire less.
This step is right. These sensory receptors send their signals through the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves.
This is the error. A fall in pressure lowers vagal tone and raises sympathetic tone.
This step is right. More sympathetic output acts on beta-1 receptor proteins in the heart and alpha-1 receptor proteins in the vessels.

why.correct: The efferent half of a visceral reflex is the two-neuron chain: the preganglionic neuron synapses in an autonomic ganglion on the postganglionic neuron.
options: Correct. The two efferent neurons meet in an autonomic ganglion.
The dorsal root ganglion holds sensory cell bodies on the afferent side, not the efferent relay.
A neuromuscular junction is where a somatic motor neuron meets skeletal muscle, the effector of a somatic reflex.
The ventral horn holds somatic motor neurons inside the CNS. The step needed is outside the CNS, between the two efferent neurons.

why.correct: Sympathetic activation narrows skin vessels (alpha-1), widens the airways (beta-2, mostly epinephrine), releases glucose from the liver (beta-2), and drives sweating (muscarinic, through cholinergic sympathetic fibers). It widens the pupils and slows the gut.
options: Correct. Norepinephrine from the vasomotor nerves acts on alpha-1 receptor proteins and contracts the smooth muscle of skin vessels.
Correct. Epinephrine on beta-2 receptor proteins makes the liver break down glycogen.
Narrowing the pupils is a parasympathetic effect. Sympathetic activity widens them through alpha-1 receptor proteins.
Correct. Sympathetic cholinergic fibers drive the eccrine sweat glands.
Speeding the gut is a parasympathetic effect. Sympathetic activity slows it.
Correct. Epinephrine relaxes airway smooth muscle through beta-2 receptor proteins.

why.correct: Parasympathetic activation slows the heart and speeds gut movement and secretion, mostly through muscarinic receptor proteins. It also relaxes the gut sphincters. Widened pupils, glucose release and sweating are sympathetic effects.
options: Correct. More vagal tone slows the heart.
Correct. This is the rest-and-digest pattern.
Widened pupils are a sympathetic effect. Parasympathetic activity narrows the pupils.
Correct. Sphincters relax, letting contents move on.
Releasing glucose from glycogen is a sympathetic effect, driven by epinephrine on beta-2 receptor proteins.
Sweat glands have no parasympathetic supply; sweating is driven by sympathetic fibers.

why.correct: The glands that make saliva have dual innervation, and here both divisions stimulate secretion. Nervousness lowers parasympathetic drive, which normally brings large volumes of watery saliva, and raises sympathetic drive, which brings a small volume of thick, protein-rich saliva.
options: Sympathetic activity does stimulate these glands, only to produce a small volume of thick saliva rather than none.
Nervousness shifts the balance toward sympathetic activity, not parasympathetic.
Correct. The change in the kind of saliva, not a total stop, makes the mouth feel sticky.
Both divisions supply these glands; they are a classic example of dual innervation.

why.correct: The hypothalamus compares temperature, water balance and energy stores with their set points, receives emotional input from the limbic system, and sends commands to the brainstem and spinal cord autonomic centers.
options: The cerebellum coordinates movement. It is not the integrator of autonomic output.
Correct. The hypothalamus sits at the top of the autonomic control hierarchy below the cerebrum.
The primary motor cortex controls voluntary movement through somatic motor pathways.
The thalamus relays sensory signals to the cortex. It does not integrate autonomic output.

why.correct: Emotional input reaches the hypothalamus from the limbic system. It can trigger a sudden rise in vagal output, which slows the heart, together with a drop in sympathetic tone, which widens the vessels. Blood pressure falls, less blood reaches the brain, and she faints.
options: Correct. This emotional pathway acts through both divisions at once.
Watching a procedure is an emotional, not a stretch, stimulus, and her own arm is not being stretched.
An epinephrine surge would speed the heart, not slow it.
The cerebellum coordinates movement. Fainting here comes from a fall in blood pressure.

why.correct: The pupillary light reflex is integrated in the midbrain: the pretectal nuclei and the Edinger–Westphal nuclei. A normal response shows the optic nerve, the midbrain and the oculomotor nerve are working.
options: The medulla oblongata integrates the reflexes of the heart, vessels and breathing, not the pupil.
The pons is not part of the pupillary light reflex pathway.
Correct. The integration center and the parasympathetic nucleus for the pupil are in the midbrain.
The cerebellum is not part of the brainstem and plays no part in this reflex.

why.correct: Brain control of all sympathetic output runs down the cord to T1–L2, below the cut. Without sympathetic tone, vessels widen (low pressure, warm pink skin) and the heart loses its sympathetic push. The vagus nerve leaves the brainstem above the cut, so vagal tone continues unopposed and slows the heart.
options: The vagus nerve leaves the brainstem and never enters the spinal cord, so a cord injury does not cut it. Losing vagal tone would speed the heart.
Epinephrine would speed the heart and constrict skin vessels, the opposite of these findings. The adrenal medulla also depends on T-segment preganglionic neurons cut off from the brain.
Correct. Lost sympathetic tone plus intact vagal tone explains all three findings.
Paralysis does not explain a slow heart or warm feet. The findings come from lost sympathetic tone.

why.correct: The adrenal medulla released epinephrine into the blood during the fright. It keeps acting on beta receptor proteins for a few minutes until it is cleared, so its effects outlast the nerve signal.
options: Correct. The hormone outlasts the burst of nerve activity.
Once the danger passes, vagal tone returns within seconds along with the fall in sympathetic firing.
Norepinephrine at a varicosity is cleared by reuptake within about a second.
Receptor proteins are not lost in a few minutes of fright.

why.correct: The hypothalamus can raise sympathetic output to the sweat glands and change its output to the skin vessels so they widen, without changing its output to the iris or the gut. Mass discharge is one mode, not the only one.
options: Mass discharge happens in emergencies, but the sympathetic division also adjusts single targets.
Correct. Temperature control uses selective sympathetic output.
Sweat glands and skin vessels have no parasympathetic supply.
Heat does not block alpha-1 receptor proteins. The pupils are unchanged because the iris is not being targeted.

why.correct: Blocking every ganglion silences both divisions. On the resting heart, vagal tone is the larger influence, so removing both leaves a net loss of braking: the heart rises toward its own rate of about 100 beats a minute.
options: Sympathetic input is removed, but the larger vagal tone is removed too, so the net effect is a rise.
The two tones are not equal at rest; vagal tone dominates.
Correct. The net loss is of the vagal brake.
The heart beats on its own; autonomic nerves only adjust its rate.

why.correct: A fall in pressure reduces the firing of the stretch-sensitive sensory receptors. The medulla oblongata responds by shifting autonomic tone: less vagal, more sympathetic. The heart speeds up and vessels narrow, bringing pressure back toward normal by negative feedback.

variables.name: Firing of stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the artery walls
variables.why: Lower pressure stretches the artery walls less, so these sensory receptors fire less.

variables.name: Vagal output to the heart
variables.why: With fewer stretch signals arriving, the medulla oblongata reduces vagal tone.

variables.name: Sympathetic output to the vessels
variables.why: The medulla oblongata increases sympathetic tone through the vasomotor nerves.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Less vagal braking and more sympathetic drive on beta-1 receptor proteins speed the heart.

variables.name: Diameter of vessels in the skin and gut
variables.why: More vasomotor firing acts on alpha-1 receptor proteins, and the vessels narrow.
